Chapter 7. The Education of the Next Generation
You know, kids have this wonderful knack for asking questions adults might not even think to ask. As the family’s experiment rolled on, the younger ones didn’t just learn—they became teachers, too. They’d spot things the grown-ups might miss, like a worm wriggling in the garden soil, or the very first crocus peeking through the snow. Even the simple act of tasting an apple straight from a neighbor’s tree turned into a little adventure. Their curiosity wove lessons into everyday moments, making chores feel like discoveries and mealtimes a chance to explore something new.
One afternoon, a child looked up and wondered—why don’t we have bananas on the table anymore? That question opened the door to a bigger conversation about how far food travels, about seasons, and about all the unseen hands that bring food to our plates. Suddenly, the family realized their experiment wasn’t just about what ended up on their table. It was about what they were passing on—lessons in patience, in gratitude, and in understanding the effort behind every bite.
The kids learned to plant tiny seeds and keep an eye out for the first signs of green. Some plants thrived, some didn’t, and that was okay—it taught them to accept a little bit of failure along the way. They picked up cooking skills, learned how to preserve the harvest, and, maybe best of all, learned how good sharing can feel. Sure, there were grumbles now and then—sometimes chores felt endless, or they missed the snacks their friends had. But there were also moments of pride. Like the day a child who’d always turned up her nose at kale suddenly couldn’t wait to share her favorite recipe. Or when the one who dreaded weeding found real satisfaction in a basket of freshly dug potatoes.
Over time, it wasn’t just about the garden. The kids started noticing things everywhere. They paid attention to waste, got braver about trying new foods, and grew more curious about where everything came from. They’d ask questions at the farmers’ market, jump in to help neighbors with their gardens, and even started projects of their own—a patch of sunflowers, a row of carrots, a jar of homemade pickles.
The adults found themselves learning from the kids, too. They saw how much easier change becomes when you meet it with curiosity instead of fear. Mistakes? Well, those just became part of the story. The family’s experiment turned into a shared adventure—one that shaped more than just their meals, but their values, and even their outlook on what’s possible.
By the end of the year, the children had grown in ways you can’t really measure on a scale or with a ruler. They learned to see food not just as something you buy, but as a story—one they were living, and one they’d carry with them for years to come.
